Judge votes✓ ✓ ✓
Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
Five datasets fit, and two of them (Porto and San Francisco) you can download today with no application. I checked these sources on 11–12 Nov 2026. Everything below is confirmed from the named page unless I mark it "from memory." I did not build the interactive shortlist page, so there is no `dataset-shortlist.html`.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** timestamped GPS points along each trip or vehicle track, not just pickup and drop-off.
- **R2 (must):** at least a few hundred vehicles, taxi or ride-hailing, any city.
- **R3 (must):** enough points per trip for trajectory similarity and for travel-time labels. Travel time can come from the first and last timestamp of a trip.
- **R4 (nice):** per-trip segmentation, an occupancy flag and a sampling interval of about 15 s or finer.
- **R5 (nice):** a licence that allows publishing results.

I assumed academic use, so I didn't weigh commercial-use clauses heavily.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Porto taxis (ECML/PKDD 2015) | Direct download, no login | CC BY 4.0 | 442 taxis, 1.71M trips, 1 year | Strong. Trips are already segmented; points every 15 s. | Today (UCI page) |
| 2 | San Francisco cabs (CRAWDAD epfl/mobility) | Free IEEE DataPort login | CC BY 4.0 | ~500 cabs, 30 days, 91 MB | Strong. Points about 10 s apart with an occupied flag, but not split into trips. | Today (IEEE DataPort) |
| 3 | T-Drive (Beijing) | Direct download via OneDrive, no registration | None stated; asks you to cite two papers | 10,357 taxis, 1 week, ~15M points | Good for scale. Sampling is coarse (about 177 s) and tracks aren't split into trips. | Today (Microsoft page) |
| 4 | Grab-Posisi (Singapore, Jakarta) | Email request, research only | No licence named; no commercial use | ~84K trajectories, >80M pings, ~2 GB | Strong. 1 s sampling. Vehicle count isn't stated on the page, so check R2. | Today (Grab page) |
| 5 | Rome taxis (CRAWDAD roma/taxi) | IEEE DataPort subscription | Not confirmed | ~320 taxis, 30 days | Good. Points every 15 s, but not segmented into trips. | Search results only |

## Details
**1. Porto: [UCI page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015)**
- **Contents:** each row is one trip. `POLYLINE` is a list of `[lon, lat]` pairs, one per 15 s. Other fields are `TAXI_ID`, `TIMESTAMP` (trip start) and call type. Per-point times are start time plus 15 s × index.
- **Steps:** click "Download (509.3 MB)" on the UCI page, or run `fetch_ucirepo(id=339)` from the `ucimlrepo` package.
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0, so attribution only.
- **Use:** Brébisson et al. won the challenge's destination-prediction task ([arXiv 1508.00021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.00021)). I didn't search for similarity or travel-time papers that use it.
- **Caveat:** the timestamps are regular by construction, so they carry no information of their own. Some trips have missing GPS segments; check this before using trip length as a label.

**2. San Francisco: [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-epflmobility)**
- **Contents:** one file per cab, each line `lat, lon, occupied, unix_time`. The occupied flag lets you cut each track into trips. Cab IDs are scrambled.
- **Steps:** create a free IEEE account, log in and download `cabspottingdata.tar.gz`. The page says both "Open Access" and "requires a DataPort subscription." My reading is that the free tier is enough, but I haven't tried the download.
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0.
- **Caveat:** the old CRAWDAD address (crawdad.org/epfl/mobility/20090224/) now returns 404, so use the IEEE DataPort page. A figshare copy ([San Francisco taxi trajectories](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302243.v1)) is listed as CC BY 4.0. I haven't checked what's different in it.

**3. T-Drive: [Microsoft Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/)**
- **Contents:** one file per taxi, each line `taxi_id, datetime, lon, lat`, covering 2–8 Feb 2008. The average gap is about 177 s (~623 m).
- **Steps:** click "Download the Trajectory Data" (OneDrive). Cite Yuan et al. (KDD '11 and GIS '10).
- **Licence:** none stated on the page. Treat it as research use with citation. I couldn't tell whether Microsoft's generic site terms apply.
- **Caveat:** a 3-minute gap is too coarse for precise route similarity unless you map-match. The data suits large-scale similarity benchmarks. Trips aren't segmented, so you would need a stay-point heuristic.

**4. Grab-Posisi: [Grab Engineering](https://engineering.grab.com/grab-posisi)**
- **Contents:** one Parquet file per trajectory with latitude, longitude, UTC timestamp, accuracy, bearing and speed at 1 s. It was collected in April 2019 from ride-hailing drivers' phones, with an Android or iOS label.
- **Steps:** email grab.posisi@grabtaxi.com with your name and contact details, your institution and your intended use. I don't have a typical turnaround; plan for days to weeks.
- **Licence:** research only, and you must cite Huang et al. 2019 ([DOI 10.1145/3356995.3364536](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3356995.3364536)). A published paper counts as research use.
- **Caveat:** the page doesn't say how many distinct drivers contributed. If you need a few hundred vehicles, ask when you email. A companion set, Grab-Posisi-L, has map-matched ground truth for 2,937 trajectories.

**5. Rome: [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi)**
- **Contents:** about 320 taxis, 1 Feb–2 Mar 2014, one point every 15 s. A user reports a 1.6 GB file of 21.8M lines. Details come from a search summary; I did not open the page.
- **Steps:** per the search summary, you need an IEEE DataPort subscription, which is free with an IEEE society membership. I did not confirm whether a plain free account is enough.
- **Licence:** not confirmed. The CRAWDAD version is cited as doi:10.15783/C7QC7M.

## Known, not confirmed
- **DiDi GAIA (Chengdu and Xi'an):** this is the best-known ride-hailing set, with driver tracks at 2–4 s sampling, order IDs, and a 2016 and an alternate 2018 release. The portal ([outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/)) returned HTTP 501 to my checker. From memory and search summaries, access is by registration and an application stating your research plan, with credit to DiDi in publications. A paper citing the portal in January 2026 suggests it was still up, but I found nothing on whether applications are currently open. Open the portal in a browser. If it's closed, use Porto and Grab-Posisi instead.
- **Bangkok taxi trajectories ([Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/17003809)):** open, CC BY 4.0, 4–24 Apr 2019, but only 33.5 MB. The page doesn't give the number of taxis, and sampling is 1–3 minutes. Check the vehicle count before relying on it.
- **Other possible sources:** Shanghai SUVnet and several Shenzhen or Shanghai files on figshare. I haven't verified their access or contents.

## Not recommended
- **[NYC telematics (Zenodo 6647220)](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220):** 16 files, about 25 MB, from a single session, with no vehicle count given. It is not a fleet.
- **GeoLife:** I didn't search for it. From memory it holds individual people's tracks rather than taxis, so it doesn't meet R2.
- **Hugging Face trajectory hits:** the HF hits ("Porto_Taxi_Trajectory", "porto_taxi") are third-party copies. Use UCI for Porto.

## What I could not find
- A trip-segmented, high-frequency (≤5 s) taxi set from several hundred vehicles with no application required. Grab-Posisi is the closest but needs an email request. DiDi would also fit but is unconfirmed.
- I didn't search for papers on how each dataset is used for similarity or travel time, beyond the Porto one above. [T-JEPA (arXiv 2406.12913)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.12913) came up in the T-Drive search, but I didn't open it to see which datasets it uses.

## Next step
Download Porto first. It is the only one that is fully open, already split into trips, and large enough. Use it to build and test your similarity and travel-time code. In parallel, email Grab for Grab-Posisi, since it has 1 s sampling and per-trip files, and register for IEEE DataPort to get San Francisco. Open the DiDi portal in a browser to see whether applications are open. Add T-Drive if you need a very large fleet and can accept the 3-minute sampling.

- **Steps:** click "Download (509.3 MB)" on the UCI page, or run `fetch_ucirepo(id=339)` from the `ucimlrepo` package.
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0, so attribution only.
- **Use:** Brébisson et al. won the challenge's destination-prediction task ([arXiv 1508.00021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.00021)). I didn't search for similarity or travel-time papers that use it.
- **Caveat:** the timestamps are regular by construction, so they carry no information of their own. Some trips have missing GPS segments; check this before using trip length as a label.

**2. San Francisco: [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-epflmobility)**
- **Contents:** one file per cab, each line `lat, lon, occupied, unix_time`. The occupied flag lets you cut each track into trips. Cab IDs are scrambled.
- **Steps:** create a free IEEE account, log in and download `cabspottingdata.tar.gz`. The page says both "Open Access" and "requires a DataPort subscription." My reading is that the free tier is enough, but I haven't tried the download.
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0.
- **Caveat:** the old CRAWDAD address (crawdad.org/epfl/mobility/20090224/) now returns 404, so use the IEEE DataPort page. A figshare copy ([San Francisco taxi trajectories](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302243.v1)) is listed as CC BY 4.0. I haven't checked what's different in it.

**3. T-Drive: [Microsoft Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/)**
- **Contents:** one file per taxi, each line `taxi_id, datetime, lon, lat`, covering 2–8 Feb 2008. The average gap is about 177 s (~623 m).
- **Steps:** click "Download the Trajectory Data" (OneDrive). Cite Yuan et al. (KDD '11 and GIS '10).
- **Licence:** none stated on the page. Treat it as research use with citation. I couldn't tell whether Microsoft's generic site terms apply.
- **Caveat:** a 3-minute gap is too coarse for precise route similarity unless you map-match. The data suits large-scale similarity benchmarks. Trips aren't segmented, so you would need a stay-point heuristic.

**4. Grab-Posisi: [Grab Engineering](https://engineering.grab.com/grab-posisi)**
- **Contents:** one Parquet file per trajectory with latitude, longitude, UTC timestamp, accuracy, bearing and speed at 1 s. It was collected in April 2019 from ride-hailing drivers' phones, with an Android or iOS label.
- **Steps:** email grab.posisi@grabtaxi.com with your name and contact details, your institution and your intended use. I don't have a typical turnaround; plan for days to weeks.
- **Licence:** research only, and you must cite Huang et al. 2019 ([DOI 10.1145/3356995.3364536](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3356995.3364536)). A published paper counts as research use.
- **Caveat:** the page doesn't say how many distinct drivers contributed. If you need a few hundred vehicles, ask when you email. A companion set, Grab-Posisi-L, has map-matched ground truth for 2,937 trajectories.

**5. Rome: [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi)**
- **Contents:** about 320 taxis, 1 Feb–2 Mar 2014, one point every 15 s. A user reports a 1.6 GB file of 21.8M lines. Details come from a search summary; I did not open the page.
- **Steps:** per the search summary, you need an IEEE DataPort subscription, which is free with an IEEE society membership. I did not confirm whether a plain free account is enough.
- **Licence:** not confirmed. The CRAWDAD version is cited as doi:10.15783/C7QC7M.

## Known, not confirmed
- **DiDi GAIA (Chengdu and Xi'an):** this is the best-known ride-hailing set, with driver tracks at 2–4 s sampling, order IDs, and a 2016 and an alternate 2018 release. The portal ([outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/)) returned HTTP 501 to my checker. From memory and search summaries, access is by registration and an application stating your research plan, with credit to DiDi in publications. A paper citing the portal in January 2026 suggests it was still up, but I found nothing on whether applications are currently open. Open the portal in a browser. If it's closed, use Porto and Grab-Posisi instead.
- **Bangkok taxi trajectories ([Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/17003809)):** open, CC BY 4.0, 4–24 Apr 2019, but only 33.5 MB. The page doesn't give the number of taxis, and sampling is 1–3 minutes. Check the vehicle count before relying on it.
- **Other possible sources:** Shanghai SUVnet and several Shenzhen or Shanghai files on figshare. I haven't verified their access or contents.

## Not recommended
- **[NYC telematics (Zenodo 6647220)](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220):** 16 files, about 25 MB, from a single session, with no vehicle count given. It is not a fleet.
- **GeoLife:** I didn't search for it. From memory it holds individual people's tracks rather than taxis, so it doesn't meet R2.
- **Hugging Face trajectory hits:** the HF hits ("Porto_Taxi_Trajectory", "porto_taxi") are third-party copies. Use UCI for Porto.

## What I could not find
- A trip-segmented, high-frequency (≤5 s) taxi set from several hundred vehicles with no application required. Grab-Posisi is the closest but needs an email request. DiDi would also fit but is unconfirmed.
- I didn't search for papers on how each dataset is used for similarity or travel time, beyond the Porto one above. [T-JEPA (arXiv 2406.12913)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.12913) came up in the T-Drive search, but I didn't open it to see which datasets it uses.

## Next step
Download Porto first. It is the only one that is fully open, already split into trips, and large enough. Use it to build and test your similarity and travel-time code. In parallel, email Grab for Grab-Posisi, since it has 1 s sampling and per-trip files, and register for IEEE DataPort to get San Francisco. Open the DiDi portal in a browser to see whether applications are open. Add T-Drive if you need a very large fleet and can accept the 3-minute sampling.

Sources:
- [UCI Porto](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015)
- [T-Drive](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/)
- [Grab-Posisi](https://engineering.grab.com/grab-posisi)
- [CRAWDAD epfl/mobility](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-epflmobility)
- [CRAWDAD roma/taxi](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi)
- [Zenodo Bangkok](https://zenodo.org/records/17003809)
- [Zenodo NYC telematics](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220)
- [DiDi GAIA portal](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/)

| 3 | T-Drive (Beijing) | Direct download via OneDrive, no registration | None stated; asks you to cite two papers | 10,357 taxis, 1 week, ~15M points | Good for scale. Sampling is coarse (about 177 s) and tracks aren't split into trips. | Today (Microsoft page) |
| 4 | Grab-Posisi (Singapore, Jakarta) | Email request, research only | No licence named; no commercial use | ~84K trajectories, >80M pings, ~2 GB | Strong. 1 s sampling. Vehicle count isn't stated on the page, so check R2. | Today (Grab page) |
| 5 | Rome taxis (CRAWDAD roma/taxi) | IEEE DataPort subscription | Not confirmed | ~320 taxis, 30 days | Good. Points every 15 s, but not segmented into trips. | Search results only |

## Details
**1. Porto: [UCI page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015)**
- **Contents:** each row is one trip. `POLYLINE` is a list of `[lon, lat]` pairs, one per 15 s. Other fields are `TAXI_ID`, `TIMESTAMP` (trip start) and call type. Per-point times are start time plus 15 s × index.
- **Steps:** click "Download (509.3 MB)" on the UCI page, or run `fetch_ucirepo(id=339)` from the `ucimlrepo` package.
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0, so attribution only.
- **Use:** Brébisson et al. won the challenge's destination-prediction task ([arXiv 1508.00021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.00021)). I didn't search for similarity or travel-time papers that use it.
- **Caveat:** the timestamps are regular by construction, so they carry no information of their own. Some trips have missing GPS segments; check this before using trip length as a label.

**2. San Francisco: [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-epflmobility)**
- **Contents:** one file per cab, each line `lat, lon, occupied, unix_time`. The occupied flag lets you cut each track into trips. Cab IDs are scrambled.
- **Steps:** create a free IEEE account, log in and download `cabspottingdata.tar.gz`. The page says both "Open Access" and "requires a DataPort subscription." My reading is that the free tier is enough, but I haven't tried the download.
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0.
- **Caveat:** the old CRAWDAD address (crawdad.org/epfl/mobility/20090224/) now returns 404, so use the IEEE DataPort page. A figshare copy ([San Francisco taxi trajectories](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302243.v1)) is listed as CC BY 4.0. I haven't checked what's different in it.

**3. T-Drive: [Microsoft Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/)**
- **Contents:** one file per taxi, each line `taxi_id, datetime, lon, lat`, covering 2–8 Feb 2008. The average gap is about 177 s (~623 m).
- **Steps:** click "Download the Trajectory Data" (OneDrive). Cite Yuan et al. (KDD '11 and GIS '10).
- **Licence:** none stated on the page. Treat it as research use with citation. I couldn't tell whether Microsoft's generic site terms apply.
- **Caveat:** a 3-minute gap is too coarse for precise route similarity unless you map-match. The data suits large-scale similarity benchmarks. Trips aren't segmented, so you would need a stay-point heuristic.

**4. Grab-Posisi: [Grab Engineering](https://engineering.grab.com/grab-posisi)**
- **Contents:** one Parquet file per trajectory with latitude, longitude, UTC timestamp, accuracy, bearing and speed at 1 s. It was collected in April 2019 from ride-hailing drivers' phones, with an Android or iOS label.
- **Steps:** email grab.posisi@grabtaxi.com with your name and contact details, your institution and your intended use. I don't have a typical turnaround; plan for days to weeks.
- **Licence:** research only, and you must cite Huang et al. 2019 ([DOI 10.1145/3356995.3364536](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3356995.3364536)). A published paper counts as research use.
- **Caveat:** the page doesn't say how many distinct drivers contributed. If you need a few hundred vehicles, ask when you email. A companion set, Grab-Posisi-L, has map-matched ground truth for 2,937 trajectories.

**5. Rome: [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi)**
- **Contents:** about 320 taxis, 1 Feb–2 Mar 2014, one point every 15 s. A user reports a 1.6 GB file of 21.8M lines. Details come from a search summary; I did not open the page.
- **Steps:** per the search summary, you need an IEEE DataPort subscription, which is free with an IEEE society membership. I did not confirm whether a plain free account is enough.
- **Licence:** not confirmed. The CRAWDAD version is cited as doi:10.15783/C7QC7M.

## Known, not confirmed
- **DiDi GAIA (Chengdu and Xi'an):** this is the best-known ride-hailing set, with driver tracks at 2–4 s sampling, order IDs, and a 2016 and an alternate 2018 release. The portal ([outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/)) returned HTTP 501 to my checker. From memory and search summaries, access is by registration and an application stating your research plan, with credit to DiDi in publications. A paper citing the portal in January 2026 suggests it was still up, but I found nothing on whether applications are currently open. Open the portal in a browser. If it's closed, use Porto and Grab-Posisi instead.
- **Bangkok taxi trajectories ([Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/17003809)):** open, CC BY 4.0, 4–24 Apr 2019, but only 33.5 MB. The page doesn't give the number of taxis, and sampling is 1–3 minutes. Check the vehicle count before relying on it.
- **Other possible sources:** Shanghai SUVnet and several Shenzhen or Shanghai files on figshare. I haven't verified their access or contents.

## Not recommended
- **[NYC telematics (Zenodo 6647220)](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220):** 16 files, about 25 MB, from a single session, with no vehicle count given. It is not a fleet.
- **GeoLife:** I didn't search for it. From memory it holds individual people's tracks rather than taxis, so it doesn't meet R2.
- **Hugging Face trajectory hits:** the HF hits ("Porto_Taxi_Trajectory", "porto_taxi") are third-party copies. Use UCI for Porto.

## What I could not find
- A trip-segmented, high-frequency (≤5 s) taxi set from several hundred vehicles with no application required. Grab-Posisi is the closest but needs an email request. DiDi would also fit but is unconfirmed.
- I didn't search for papers on how each dataset is used for similarity or travel time, beyond the Porto one above. [T-JEPA (arXiv 2406.12913)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.12913) came up in the T-Drive search, but I didn't open it to see which datasets it uses.

## Next step
Download Porto first. It is the only one that is fully open, already split into trips, and large enough. Use it to build and test your similarity and travel-time code. In parallel, email Grab for Grab-Posisi, since it has 1 s sampling and per-trip files, and register for IEEE DataPort to get San Francisco. Open the DiDi portal in a browser to see whether applications are open. Add T-Drive if you need a very large fleet and can accept the 3-minute sampling.

- [Zenodo NYC telematics](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220)
- [DiDi GAIA portal](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/)

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
Four datasets fit what you described, and three of them you can download today. Each has full timestamped point sequences from at least several hundred vehicles. I checked them on 2026-11-12, and the sources are noted per dataset.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** timestamped GPS point sequences along each trip, not just pickup and drop-off.
- **R2 (must):** at least a few hundred vehicles, in any city.
- **R3 (must):** usable for trajectory similarity and travel-time estimation. That means a fixed trip start and end, or enough points to cut trips yourself.
- **R4 (nice):** downloadable now, with a licence that allows research use.

## Shortlist

| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Porto taxi trajectories (ECML/PKDD 2015) | Direct download, no account stated | CC BY 4.0 | 442 taxis, 1.71M trips, one point every 15 s | Today, UCI page |
| 2 | T-Drive, Beijing | Download from a Microsoft Research page (hosted on OneDrive) | None stated; citation requested | 10,357 taxis, about 15M points, one week in Feb 2008, about 177 s between points | Today |
| 3 | Rome taxi (CRAWDAD roma/taxi) | Free IEEE DataPort account | CC BY 4.0 | About 320 taxis, 30 days, about 374 MB compressed | Today, partly |
| 4 | Didi GAIA, Chengdu and Xi'an | Registration or application to Didi | Didi terms of use | Chengdu has about 1.1M drivers, Nov 2016 | Partly, from search results |

## Details

**1. Porto.** This is the safest start. Each trip is one row with a `POLYLINE` of `[lon, lat]` pairs and a `TIMESTAMP`. The sampling is regular at 15 s, so each point's time is trip start plus 15 s times its index. Trip start and end are explicit.
- **Access:** download `train.csv.zip` (about 509 MB) from the [UCI page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015), or run `pip install ucimlrepo` and call `fetch_ucirepo(id=339)`. The page shows only an optional login link.
- **Mirrors:** there are copies on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Davidham3/Porto_Taxi_Trajectory) (Apache-2.0, ungated) and [figshare](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302165.v1) (CC BY 4.0). The UCI copy is the original, so use that one.
- **Caveats:** `MISSING_DATA` flags gaps in some trips. The data has trip-level timestamps and fixed 15 s spacing rather than per-point times.
- **Use:** it is the standard benchmark for travel-time and destination prediction, and I recall (not checked today) that it is common in trajectory-similarity papers.

**2. T-Drive.**
- **Contents:** one text file per taxi, with lines of `taxi_id, datetime, lon, lat`.
- **Access:** the [Microsoft Research page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/) has a "Download the Trajectory Data" link. The page states no registration and no licence, only a request to cite the KDD '11 and GIS '10 papers. The [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf) may say more, and I didn't read it.
- **Caveats:** there are no trip boundaries, so you have to split trips yourself. The long gaps between points (about 177 s) are poor for fine-grained similarity. That is also why it is a good test of sparse-trajectory methods.
- **Copies to avoid:** some secondary descriptions of this dataset (6 months, 30,000 taxis) don't match Microsoft's own description. The [TIB record](https://doi.org/10.57702/enayhf6y) returned a 404. The [IEEE DataPort "POETIC – Tdrive and nyc"](https://doi.org/10.21227/rgbn-cw81) copy needs a subscription.

**3. Rome.** Lines look like `DRIVER_ID;TIMESTAMP;POINT(lat lon)`, sorted by time. The data was originally on CRAWDAD and is now on [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi). The page says open access but also that a logged-in account is needed, and one line mentions a "subscription". A free IEEE account is probably enough, but confirm this when you download.
- **Caveats:** there are no trip IDs, so you have to segment trips. The sampling interval is inconsistent between sources (the page says 7 s, another source says 15 s). Check this against the data.

**4. Didi GAIA (Chengdu and Xi'an, Oct/Nov 2016).** This is the largest source and the closest to ride-hailing. Records have driver ID, order ID, timestamp, lon and lat. It is the only one here that is ride-hailing rather than taxi data.
- **Access:** the portal is [outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/). My fetch returned HTTP 501, so I could not read the form.
- **What I found:** a PLOS ONE paper says you can access it after free registration. A 2026 MDPI paper says it is available from Didi for academic research under their terms, and that derived data can only be shared with Didi's permission.
- **Before you plan around it:** confirm today whether the portal is still accepting requests, how long approval takes, and whether the terms restrict redistribution.

## Known, not confirmed
- **San Francisco Cabspotting.** I recall about 500 taxis with timestamped GPS from the original CRAWDAD epfl/mobility trace. There is a [figshare copy](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302243.v1) with a CC BY 4.0 record, but I couldn't open the landing page. Its terms may differ from the original's, so check them before relying on it.
- **Shenzhen and Shanghai taxi datasets** (for example [Pingshan, Shenzhen](https://doi.org/10.13140/rg.2.2.20676.80007), [Shanghai taxi demand/flow](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31481464.v2)). The DOIs are real but both landing pages blocked me. The Shanghai one may be aggregated flows rather than raw points. The Pingshan one covers a single day. I haven't checked either one's size or fit.
- **Bangkok taxi trajectories on Zenodo** ([tourist trajectories](https://zenodo.org/records/17005200) and [segmented trips](https://zenodo.org/records/17003809)). Both are open under CC BY 4.0 (confirmed). They look like derived subsets, and I didn't check the vehicle count.

## Not recommended
- **IEEE DataPort "Taxi trajectories"** ([10.21227/rxw4-1r28](https://doi.org/10.21227/rxw4-1r28)): it needs a paid subscription, and the file names look like NYC 2015 taxi data, which is pickup and drop-off only.
- **NYC TLC trip records:** pickup and drop-off only.
- **GeoLife:** about 180 users, not taxis.
- **The [NYC telematics Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220):** I verified that it exists but not its contents, so I left it out.

## What I could not find
- **Several searches returned nothing relevant.** The "ride-hailing GPS" query returned nothing useful from DataCite, OpenAIRE and Zenodo.
- **Pages I couldn't open.** Didi's portal gave a server error, and the original CRAWDAD page returned 404. Neither Didi's current terms nor T-Drive's user-guide terms were read.
- **No evidence-of-use check.** I did not run the step that finds papers using each dataset. The literature search returned only generic surveys, so I can't point you to similarity or ETA baselines from this session.
- **No HTML shortlist page.** I skipped it because this reply covers the same content.

## Next step
1. Start with Porto, since it is clean and open and has a known benchmark setup.
2. Add Rome or T-Drive for a second city with a different sampling rate.
3. Apply to Didi now if you want ride-hailing data, because approval may take time.

The data was originally on CRAWDAD and is now on [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi). The page says open access but also that a logged-in account is needed, and one line mentions a "subscription". A free IEEE account is probably enough, but confirm this when you download.
- **Caveats:** there are no trip IDs, so you have to segment trips. The sampling interval is inconsistent between sources (the page says 7 s, another source says 15 s). Check this against the data.

**4. Didi GAIA (Chengdu and Xi'an, Oct/Nov 2016).** This is the largest source and the closest to ride-hailing. Records have driver ID, order ID, timestamp, lon and lat. It is the only one here that is ride-hailing rather than taxi data.
- **Access:** the portal is [outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/). My fetch returned HTTP 501, so I could not read the form.
- **What I found:** a PLOS ONE paper says you can access it after free registration. A 2026 MDPI paper says it is available from Didi for academic research under their terms, and that derived data can only be shared with Didi's permission.
- **Before you plan around it:** confirm today whether the portal is still accepting requests, how long approval takes, and whether the terms restrict redistribution.

## Known, not confirmed
- **San Francisco Cabspotting.** I recall about 500 taxis with timestamped GPS from the original CRAWDAD epfl/mobility trace. There is a [figshare copy](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302243.v1) with a CC BY 4.0 record, but I couldn't open the landing page. Its terms may differ from the original's, so check them before relying on it.
- **Shenzhen and Shanghai taxi datasets** (for example [Pingshan, Shenzhen](https://doi.org/10.13140/rg.2.2.20676.80007), [Shanghai taxi demand/flow](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31481464.v2)). The DOIs are real but both landing pages blocked me. The Shanghai one may be aggregated flows rather than raw points. The Pingshan one covers a single day. I haven't checked either one's size or fit.
- **Bangkok taxi trajectories on Zenodo** ([tourist trajectories](https://zenodo.org/records/17005200) and [segmented trips](https://zenodo.org/records/17003809)). Both are open under CC BY 4.0 (confirmed). They look like derived subsets, and I didn't check the vehicle count.

## Not recommended
- **IEEE DataPort "Taxi trajectories"** ([10.21227/rxw4-1r28](https://doi.org/10.21227/rxw4-1r28)): it needs a paid subscription, and the file names look like NYC 2015 taxi data, which is pickup and drop-off only.
- **NYC TLC trip records:** pickup and drop-off only.
- **GeoLife:** about 180 users, not taxis.
- **The [NYC telematics Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220):** I verified that it exists but not its contents, so I left it out.

## What I could not find
- **Several searches returned nothing relevant.** The "ride-hailing GPS" query returned nothing useful from DataCite, OpenAIRE and Zenodo.
- **Pages I couldn't open.** Didi's portal gave a server error, and the original CRAWDAD page returned 404. Neither Didi's current terms nor T-Drive's user-guide terms were read.
- **No evidence-of-use check.** I did not run the step that finds papers using each dataset. The literature search returned only generic surveys, so I can't point you to similarity or ETA baselines from this session.
- **No HTML shortlist page.** I skipped it because this reply covers the same content.

1. Start with Porto, since it is clean and open and has a known benchmark setup.

| 2 | T-Drive, Beijing | Download from a Microsoft Research page (hosted on OneDrive) | None stated; citation requested | 10,357 taxis, about 15M points, one week in Feb 2008, about 177 s between points | Today |
| 3 | Rome taxi (CRAWDAD roma/taxi) | Free IEEE DataPort account | CC BY 4.0 | About 320 taxis, 30 days, about 374 MB compressed | Today, partly |
| 4 | Didi GAIA, Chengdu and Xi'an | Registration or application to Didi | Didi terms of use | Chengdu has about 1.1M drivers, Nov 2016 | Partly, from search results |

## Details

**1. Porto.** This is the safest start. Each trip is one row with a `POLYLINE` of `[lon, lat]` pairs and a `TIMESTAMP`. The sampling is regular at 15 s, so each point's time is trip start plus 15 s times its index. Trip start and end are explicit.
- **Access:** download `train.csv.zip` (about 509 MB) from the [UCI page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015), or run `pip install ucimlrepo` and call `fetch_ucirepo(id=339)`. The page shows only an optional login link.
- **Mirrors:** there are copies on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Davidham3/Porto_Taxi_Trajectory) (Apache-2.0, ungated) and [figshare](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302165.v1) (CC BY 4.0). The UCI copy is the original, so use that one.
- **Caveats:** `MISSING_DATA` flags gaps in some trips. The data has trip-level timestamps and fixed 15 s spacing rather than per-point times.
- **Use:** it is the standard benchmark for travel-time and destination prediction, and I recall (not checked today) that it is common in trajectory-similarity papers.

**2. T-Drive.**
- **Contents:** one text file per taxi, with lines of `taxi_id, datetime, lon, lat`.
- **Access:** the [Microsoft Research page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/) has a "Download the Trajectory Data" link. The page states no registration and no licence, only a request to cite the KDD '11 and GIS '10 papers. The [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf) may say more, and I didn't read it.
- **Caveats:** there are no trip boundaries, so you have to split trips yourself. The long gaps between points (about 177 s) are poor for fine-grained similarity. That is also why it is a good test of sparse-trajectory methods.
- **Copies to avoid:** some secondary descriptions of this dataset (6 months, 30,000 taxis) don't match Microsoft's own description. The [TIB record](https://doi.org/10.57702/enayhf6y) returned a 404. The [IEEE DataPort "POETIC – Tdrive and nyc"](https://doi.org/10.21227/rgbn-cw81) copy needs a subscription.

**3. Rome.** Lines look like `DRIVER_ID;TIMESTAMP;POINT(lat lon)`, sorted by time. The data was originally on CRAWDAD and is now on [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi). The page says open access but also that a logged-in account is needed, and one line mentions a "subscription". A free IEEE account is probably enough, but confirm this when you download.
- **Caveats:** there are no trip IDs, so you have to segment trips. The sampling interval is inconsistent between sources (the page says 7 s, another source says 15 s). Check this against the data.

**4. Didi GAIA (Chengdu and Xi'an, Oct/Nov 2016).** This is the largest source and the closest to ride-hailing. Records have driver ID, order ID, timestamp, lon and lat. It is the only one here that is ride-hailing rather than taxi data.
- **Access:** the portal is [outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/). My fetch returned HTTP 501, so I could not read the form.
- **What I found:** a PLOS ONE paper says you can access it after free registration. A 2026 MDPI paper says it is available from Didi for academic research under their terms, and that derived data can only be shared with Didi's permission.
- **Before you plan around it:** confirm today whether the portal is still accepting requests, how long approval takes, and whether the terms restrict redistribution.

## Known, not confirmed
- **San Francisco Cabspotting.** I recall about 500 taxis with timestamped GPS from the original CRAWDAD epfl/mobility trace. There is a [figshare copy](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302243.v1) with a CC BY 4.0 record, but I couldn't open the landing page. Its terms may differ from the original's, so check them before relying on it.
- **Shenzhen and Shanghai taxi datasets** (for example [Pingshan, Shenzhen](https://doi.org/10.13140/rg.2.2.20676.80007), [Shanghai taxi demand/flow](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31481464.v2)). The DOIs are real but both landing pages blocked me. The Shanghai one may be aggregated flows rather than raw points. The Pingshan one covers a single day. I haven't checked either one's size or fit.
- **Bangkok taxi trajectories on Zenodo** ([tourist trajectories](https://zenodo.org/records/17005200) and [segmented trips](https://zenodo.org/records/17003809)). Both are open under CC BY 4.0 (confirmed). They look like derived subsets, and I didn't check the vehicle count.

## Not recommended
- **IEEE DataPort "Taxi trajectories"** ([10.21227/rxw4-1r28](https://doi.org/10.21227/rxw4-1r28)): it needs a paid subscription, and the file names look like NYC 2015 taxi data, which is pickup and drop-off only.
- **NYC TLC trip records:** pickup and drop-off only.
- **GeoLife:** about 180 users, not taxis.
- **The [NYC telematics Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220):** I verified that it exists but not its contents, so I left it out.

## What I could not find
- **Several searches returned nothing relevant.** The "ride-hailing GPS" query returned nothing useful from DataCite, OpenAIRE and Zenodo.
- **Pages I couldn't open.** Didi's portal gave a server error, and the original CRAWDAD page returned 404. Neither Didi's current terms nor T-Drive's user-guide terms were read.
- **No evidence-of-use check.** I did not run the step that finds papers using each dataset. The literature search returned only generic surveys, so I can't point you to similarity or ETA baselines from this session.
- **No HTML shortlist page.** I skipped it because this reply covers the same content.

## Next step
1. Start with Porto, since it is clean and open and has a known benchmark setup.
2. Add Rome or T-Drive for a second city with a different sampling rate.
3. Apply to Didi now if you want ride-hailing data, because approval may take time.

| 2 | CRAWDAD epfl/mobility (San Francisco cabs) | Free IEEE DataPort account | Not stated on the page; no-deanonymisation clause | ~500 cabs, 25–30 days, ~11M points | Strong | Today |
| 3 | CRAWDAD roma/taxi (Rome) | Free IEEE DataPort account | Not stated on the page; no-deanonymisation clause | ~320 taxis, ~30 days, 15 s | Strong | Today (access); contents from search |

## Details

**1. Porto.** All trips are in one CSV, one row per completed trip. Each row has a `POLYLINE` of GPS points, taxi ID, start timestamp, and call type.
- **Access:** take it from the [UCI page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015). The challenge's own page is at geolink.pt, and Kaggle has a copy of the competition data. The UCI page confirms 442 taxis, 1,710,671 trips and 2013-07-01 to 2014-06-30. The 15 s sampling interval came from a web search summary, not from the page itself.
- **Travel time:** trip duration is (number of points − 1) × 15 s, so it needs no separate label.
- **Caveats:** UCI says the data has missing values. Some papers report missing GPS updates, so filter trips with too few points.
- **Papers using it:** [first-place neural-network solution](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.00021) and [BlueTaxi](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.05257), which also covers trip-time prediction.
- **Don't use the figshare "Porto taxi trajectories" record.** It keeps only the origin and destination of each trip (checked in its record). The Hugging Face copies are unofficial and I didn't check them.

**2. San Francisco (Cabspotting).**
- **Access:** create a free IEEE DataPort account, log in at [the dataset page](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-epflmobility), and download `cabspottingdata.tar.gz` (about 91 MB). I confirmed this today. The DOI is 10.15783/C7J010.
- **Contents:** one file per cab, with latitude, longitude, an occupied flag and a Unix timestamp. These details are from search results.
- **Licence:** the page states no licence. It asks you not to try to re-identify people.
- **Don't use the figshare "San Francisco taxi trajectories" record.** It is also origin/destination only.

**3. Rome.**
- **Access:** same route as San Francisco, using a free IEEE DataPort login on [the roma/taxi page](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi). I confirmed the login requirement today. The DOI is 10.15783/C7QC7M.
- **Contents:** about 320 taxis in central Rome, roughly February to March 2014, with taxi ID, timestamp, latitude and longitude (from search results, not confirmed).
- **Licence:** none stated. The same no-deanonymisation clause applies.

**4. T-Drive.**
- **Access:** use the "Download the Trajectory Data" link on the [Microsoft Research page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/). I saw the link there today. The [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf) asks you to cite the two Yuan et al. papers.
- **Licence:** I couldn't confirm any licence terms.
- **Why partial:** the average gap is about 3 minutes and about 600 m. That is too coarse for good point-level similarity or segment-level travel times. It is fine for coarse similarity benchmarks.
- **Don't trust the six-month claim.** One arXiv paper says six months, but Microsoft's page says one week (2–8 February 2008).

**5. DiDi GAIA.**
- **What it holds:** ride-hailing trajectories and orders for Chengdu (November 2016) and Xi'an (October to November 2016), with later 2018 releases, sampled about every 3 s. That comes from papers, not the official page.
- **Access:** the data is on DiDi's Open Data portal, `outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/`. Older papers describe free registration. A January 2026 GitHub note says you now apply and agree to DiDi's terms. Expect an application and approval step, but I couldn't confirm the wait or the licence.
- **Status:** the official page returned HTTP 501 to me, and I found no announcement of a shutdown. Confirm it's live before you plan around it. Don't use mirrors of this data.
- **Papers using it:** the [Annals of GIS floating-car study](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19475683.2023.2166109) and [RouteKG](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03617).

**6. Grab-Posisi.**
- **Access:** email grab.posisi@grabtaxi.com with your name, institution and intended use. The [dataset page is here](https://engineering.grab.com/grab-posisi) and the [paper is here](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3356995.3364536).
- **Terms:** non-commercial use only.
- **Contents:** one Parquet file per trajectory, about 2 GB in total, with 1 s pings that include speed and bearing. This is Southeast Asian ride-hailing data from search results.
- **What I didn't confirm:** whether the programme is still answering requests.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Shanghai taxi data:** the [TaxiSH figshare record](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31481464.v2) is CC BY 4.0, but it's an aggregated 1 km grid of flows derived from 2.16 billion GPS records. It is not raw trajectories, so I'd skip it.
- **Pingshan District, Shenzhen:** [one day of taxi GPS trips](https://doi.org/10.13140/rg.2.2.20676.80007), hosted on ResearchGate. No licence or access terms are stated, and I couldn't confirm the contents.
- **Bangkok:** [segmented taxi trajectories](https://zenodo.org/records/17005200) on Zenodo, CC BY 4.0, open, from the ITIC Foundation's taxi probe data. I didn't check the sampling or fleet size. The ITIC original may offer more.
- **Shanghai SUVnet taxi traces:** from memory, these are available only by application to the Shanghai Jiao Tong University group. I didn't search for them.

## Not recommended
- **GeoLife:** it records walkers and cyclists, not taxis.
- **NYC TLC trip records:** they have pickup and drop-off only.
- **Uber Movement:** it publishes aggregated travel times, with no points.
- **Zenodo "NYC telematics data":** it comes from instrumented research cars on 15 to 30 minute drives, not a taxi fleet.

## What I could not find
- A clean official-page confirmation of the Porto licence.
- Any licence terms for T-Drive, San Francisco or Rome.
- Whether DiDi GAIA and Grab-Posisi are accepting requests today.

## Next step
Start with Porto, which is open and well suited to both of your tasks. Add San Francisco and Rome the same day with a free IEEE DataPort login. Email Grab and apply to DiDi now, since those two take time.

- **Licence:** the page states no licence. It asks you not to try to re-identify people.
- **Don't use the figshare "San Francisco taxi trajectories" record.** It is also origin/destination only.

**3. Rome.**
- **Access:** same route as San Francisco, using a free IEEE DataPort login on [the roma/taxi page](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi). I confirmed the login requirement today. The DOI is 10.15783/C7QC7M.

- **Licence:** none stated. The same no-deanonymisation clause applies.

**4. T-Drive.**
- **Access:** use the "Download the Trajectory Data" link on the [Microsoft Research page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/). I saw the link there today. The [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf) asks you to cite the two Yuan et al. papers.

**5. DiDi GAIA.**

- **Shanghai taxi data:** the [TaxiSH figshare record](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31481464.v2) is CC BY 4.0, but it's an aggregated 1 km grid of flows derived from 2.16 billion GPS records. It is not raw trajectories, so I'd skip it.

- **Bangkok:** [segmented taxi trajectories](https://zenodo.org/records/17005200) on Zenodo, CC BY 4.0, open, from the ITIC Foundation's taxi probe data. I didn't check the sampling or fleet size. The ITIC original may offer more.

A January 2026 GitHub note says you now apply and agree to DiDi's terms. Expect an application and approval step, but I couldn't confirm the wait or the licence.

**6. Grab-Posisi.**
- **Access:** email grab.posisi@grabtaxi.com with your name, institution and intended use. The [dataset page is here](https://engineering.grab.com/grab-posisi) and the [paper is here](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3356995.3364536).
- **Terms:** non-commercial use only.
- **Contents:** one Parquet file per trajectory, about 2 GB in total, with 1 s pings that include speed and bearing. This is Southeast Asian ride-hailing data from search results.
- **What I didn't confirm:** whether the programme is still answering requests.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Shanghai taxi data:** the [TaxiSH figshare record](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31481464.v2) is CC BY 4.0, but it's an aggregated 1 km grid of flows derived from 2.16 billion GPS records. It is not raw trajectories, so I'd skip it.
- **Pingshan District, Shenzhen:** [one day of taxi GPS trips](https://doi.org/10.13140/rg.2.2.20676.80007), hosted on ResearchGate. No licence or access terms are stated, and I couldn't confirm the contents.
- **Bangkok:** [segmented taxi trajectories](https://zenodo.org/records/17005200) on Zenodo, CC BY 4.0, open, from the ITIC Foundation's taxi probe data. I didn't check the sampling or fleet size. The ITIC original may offer more.
- **Shanghai SUVnet taxi traces:** from memory, these are available only by application to the Shanghai Jiao Tong University group. I didn't search for them.

## Not recommended
- **GeoLife:** it records walkers and cyclists, not taxis.
- **NYC TLC trip records:** they have pickup and drop-off only.
- **Uber Movement:** it publishes aggregated travel times, with no points.
- **Zenodo "NYC telematics data":** it comes from instrumented research cars on 15 to 30 minute drives, not a taxi fleet.

- A clean official-page confirmation of the Porto licence.

The best fit is the Porto taxi dataset: 442 taxis with a GPS point every 15 seconds along every trip, and you can download it today. Four more have full point sequences from a few hundred vehicles or more: T-Drive, DiDi GAIA, San Francisco and Rome. Grab-Posisi also has them but isn't a taxi dataset (see its row). The registries (Zenodo, DataCite, OpenAIRE, Hugging Face) mostly returned noise, so the datasets below come from web search. I did not build the interactive shortlist page.

I checked these on 2026-11-11. "Confirmed" means I read it today from the source named. "Memory" means I believe it but didn't confirm it.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** timestamped GPS points along each trip, not only pickup and drop-off.
- **R2 (must):** at least a few hundred vehicles, taxi or ride-hailing, any city.
- **R3 (nice):** a sampling interval fine enough for travel-time estimation and similarity measures.
- **R4 (nice):** downloadable today. I assumed you're doing academic, non-commercial work.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Porto taxi (ECML/PKDD 2015) | Direct download | CC BY 4.0 (memory; UCI page's licence text didn't load) | 442 taxis, 1.71M trips, 1 year, point every 15 s | Strong | Today (contents); licence from memory |
| 2 | CRAWDAD epfl/mobility (San Francisco cabs) | Free IEEE DataPort account | Not stated on the page; no-deanonymisation clause | ~500 cabs, 25–30 days, ~11M points | Strong | Today |
| 3 | CRAWDAD roma/taxi (Rome) | Free IEEE DataPort account | Not stated on the page; no-deanonymisation clause | ~320 taxis, ~30 days, 15 s | Strong | Today (access); contents from search |
| 4 | T-Drive (Beijing) | Download link on Microsoft Research page | Not confirmed; citation requested | 10,357 taxis, 1 week, ~15M points, ~177 s average gap | Partial: sparse sampling | Today (page); details from search |
| 5 | DiDi GAIA (Chengdu, Xi'an) | Application and approval (memory) | DiDi's terms (memory) | Millions of orders, ~3 s sampling (per papers) | Strong if you get it | Not confirmed: official site returned HTTP 501 |
| 6 | Grab-Posisi (Singapore, Jakarta) | Email request, a few days to weeks | Non-commercial | ~84K trajectories, 80M+ pings, 1 s | Strong | From search results only |

## Details

**1. Porto.** All trips are in one CSV, one row per completed trip. Each row has a `POLYLINE` of GPS points, taxi ID, start timestamp, and call type.
- **Access:** take it from the [UCI page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015). The challenge's own page is at geolink.pt, and Kaggle has a copy of the competition data. The UCI page confirms 442 taxis, 1,710,671 trips and 2013-07-01 to 2014-06-30. The 15 s sampling interval came from a web search summary, not from the page itself.
- **Travel time:** trip duration is (number of points − 1) × 15 s, so it needs no separate label.
- **Caveats:** UCI says the data has missing values. Some papers report missing GPS updates, so filter trips with too few points.
- **Papers using it:** [first-place neural-network solution](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.00021) and [BlueTaxi](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.05257), which also covers trip-time prediction.
- **Don't use the figshare "Porto taxi trajectories" record.** It keeps only the origin and destination of each trip (checked in its record). The Hugging Face copies are unofficial and I didn't check them.

**2. San Francisco (Cabspotting).**
- **Access:** create a free IEEE DataPort account, log in at [the dataset page](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-epflmobility), and download `cabspottingdata.tar.gz` (about 91 MB). I confirmed this today. The DOI is 10.15783/C7J010.
- **Contents:** one file per cab, with latitude, longitude, an occupied flag and a Unix timestamp. These details are from search results.
- **Licence:** the page states no licence. It asks you not to try to re-identify people.
- **Don't use the figshare "San Francisco taxi trajectories" record.** It is also origin/destination only.

**3. Rome.**
- **Access:** same route as San Francisco, using a free IEEE DataPort login on [the roma/taxi page](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi). I confirmed the login requirement today. The DOI is 10.15783/C7QC7M.
- **Contents:** about 320 taxis in central Rome, roughly February to March 2014, with taxi ID, timestamp, latitude and longitude (from search results, not confirmed).
- **Licence:** none stated. The same no-deanonymisation clause applies.

**4. T-Drive.**
- **Access:** use the "Download the Trajectory Data" link on the [Microsoft Research page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/). I saw the link there today. The [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf) asks you to cite the two Yuan et al. papers.
- **Licence:** I couldn't confirm any licence terms.
- **Why partial:** the average gap is about 3 minutes and about 600 m. That is too coarse for good point-level similarity or segment-level travel times. It is fine for coarse similarity benchmarks.
- **Don't trust the six-month claim.** One arXiv paper says six months, but Microsoft's page says one week (2–8 February 2008).

**5. DiDi GAIA.**

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
I'm answering from memory and haven't checked the links or access terms this session. Check each landing page before you build on it, since hosting and access rules change.

| Dataset | City / scale | Sampling | What you do to get it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Porto (ECML/PKDD 2015)** | Porto; 442 taxis, about 1.7M trips, Jul 2013–Jun 2014 | One point every 15 s, stored per trip | Download it from the UCI ML Repository with no signup. It's also on Kaggle, where you need a free account and have to accept the competition rules. |
| **T-Drive (Microsoft Research)** | Beijing; 10,357 taxis, about 15M points, one week in Feb 2008 | Irregular, about 3 min on average | Download it from the Microsoft Research page. It's a free direct download, and the page asks you to cite the T-Drive papers. |
| **DiDi GAIA Open Data** | Chengdu and Xi'an, Oct–Nov 2016; Haikou has also been listed | About 2–4 s | Apply on the DiDi Gaia research portal with an institutional affiliation and a stated research purpose. Approval is manual and usually restricted to non-commercial use. Access has been inconsistent over time. |
| **San Francisco Cabspotting (CRAWDAD `epfl/mobility`)** | San Francisco; about 536 taxis, about 30 days in May 2008 | About 1 min | Register with CRAWDAD and accept its license. The archive has moved hosts over the years, so look for the current location. It includes an occupancy flag. |
| **Rome taxi (CRAWDAD `roma/taxi`)** | Rome; about 320 taxis, 30 days in Feb 2014 | A few seconds to tens of seconds | Same CRAWDAD registration and license as above. |
| **Grab-Posisi** | Southeast Asia (Singapore, Jakarta) | Varies | It was released for a Grab research challenge. I'm not sure it's still available, so check before planning around it. |

NYC TLC and Chicago taxi data are the well-known ones, but they only have pickup and drop-off, so they don't fit your needs.

**Which to use**
- **Travel-time estimation:** Porto. Trips are already segmented, so you get a ground-truth duration (points × 15 s) and a start timestamp, taxi ID, and day type. It's the standard benchmark for this task.
- **Trajectory similarity:** Porto and T-Drive are both common. T-Drive's sparse, irregular sampling makes it a good robustness test. DiDi Chengdu/Xi'an is the dense option if you get approved.

**Caveats**
- **Porto:** The timestamp field is only the trip start. You reconstruct per-point times from the 15 s interval, and some trips have missing points or are very short.
- **T-Drive:** Each file is one taxi's continuous stream, with no trip boundaries or occupancy flag. You have to segment trips yourself, for example by time gaps.
- **CRAWDAD:** Its licenses generally bar redistributing the data, so you can't republish it.

I can pull the current download pages and confirm the access steps and licenses if you want.

Judge votes✓ ✓ ✓
Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
I'm going from memory rather than live-checking the pages, so confirm the links, license terms and sizes before you commit to one. Hosting for older datasets (CRAWDAD especially) has moved over the years.

## Easiest to get, no approval needed

| Dataset | Scale and sampling | What you have to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Porto taxi (ECML/PKDD 2015)** | 442 taxis, about 1.7M trips, July 2013 to June 2014. One GPS point every 15 s, stored as a `POLYLINE` of lon/lat per trip. | Download it from the UCI ML Repository, which needs no login. The Kaggle copy needs a Kaggle account and acceptance of the competition rules. |
| **T-Drive (Microsoft Research, Beijing)** | 10,357 taxis, one week in Feb 2008, about 15M points. Sampling is sparse, around 3 minutes on average. | Download it from the Microsoft Research page, which is free. They ask you to cite the T-Drive papers. |

## Registration or a request required

| Dataset | Scale and sampling | What you have to do |
|---|---|---|
| **San Francisco "epfl/mobility" (Cabspotting)** | 536 taxis, about 30 days in May 2008. Points arrive roughly every minute, with an **occupancy flag**. | It's hosted via CRAWDAD. Create an account, accept the data-use terms, and download. Check whether it has moved to IEEE DataPort. |
| **Rome taxi (CRAWDAD `roma/taxi`)** | 320 taxis, 30 days in Feb 2014, about 7 s sampling. | Same CRAWDAD process as above. |
| **Didi GAIA Open Data (Chengdu and Xi'an)** | Ride-hailing cars, Oct to Nov 2016. Sampling is about 2 to 4 s, so very dense. | Apply on the GAIA site with your institution and project description. Approval is manual, and you agree not to redistribute. Availability has been inconsistent, so check it's currently accepting applications. |
| **Shanghai taxi (SUVnet)** | Several thousand taxis. | Email the SJTU group that maintains it and state your academic purpose. Response times vary. |

## Which to use

- **Trajectory similarity:** Porto and T-Drive are the standard benchmarks, so your results will be comparable with published work.
- **Travel-time estimation:** Porto is the practical choice. Trip duration is (number of points − 1) × 15 s, and trips are already segmented. Didi is better if you can get it, because its dense sampling supports finer-grained road-level work.

## Caveats

- **Porto:** some trips have `MISSING_DATA=True`, and others have GPS jumps. Filter these first. It has no map-matching, so you'll need OSM plus something like Valhalla or FMM if you want road segments.
- **T-Drive:** it's continuous per-taxi logs with no trip boundaries or occupancy flag. You'd have to segment trips yourself. The sampling is also too sparse for fine-grained similarity.
- **San Francisco:** the occupancy flag lets you split trips cleanly, but the sampling is coarse.

**Skip** NYC TLC, Chicago and Uber Movement. They only have pickup/drop-off or aggregated speeds, not point sequences. GeoLife has real trajectories but comes from 182 people, mostly walking and transit, not taxis.

Porto alone meets your "few hundred vehicles" bar, so I'd start there. Add T-Drive or Didi for cross-city generalization. I can write a loader and cleaning script for Porto if that would help.

| **T-Drive (Microsoft Research, Beijing)** | 10,357 taxis, one week in Feb 2008, about 15M points. Sampling is sparse, around 3 minutes on average. | Download it from the Microsoft Research page, which is free. They ask you to cite the T-Drive papers. |

## Registration or a request required

| Dataset | Scale and sampling | What you have to do |
|---|---|---|
| **San Francisco "epfl/mobility" (Cabspotting)** | 536 taxis, about 30 days in May 2008. Points arrive roughly every minute, with an **occupancy flag**. | It's hosted via CRAWDAD. Create an account, accept the data-use terms, and download. Check whether it has moved to IEEE DataPort. |
| **Rome taxi (CRAWDAD `roma/taxi`)** | 320 taxis, 30 days in Feb 2014, about 7 s sampling. | Same CRAWDAD process as above. |
| **Didi GAIA Open Data (Chengdu and Xi'an)** | Ride-hailing cars, Oct to Nov 2016. Sampling is about 2 to 4 s, so very dense. | Apply on the GAIA site with your institution and project description. Approval is manual, and you agree not to redistribute. Availability has been inconsistent, so check it's currently accepting applications. |
| **Shanghai taxi (SUVnet)** | Several thousand taxis. | Email the SJTU group that maintains it and state your academic purpose. Response times vary. |

## Which to use

- **Trajectory similarity:** Porto and T-Drive are the standard benchmarks, so your results will be comparable with published work.
- **Travel-time estimation:** Porto is the practical choice. Trip duration is (number of points − 1) × 15 s, and trips are already segmented. Didi is better if you can get it, because its dense sampling supports finer-grained road-level work.

## Caveats

- **Porto:** some trips have `MISSING_DATA=True`, and others have GPS jumps. Filter these first. It has no map-matching, so you'll need OSM plus something like Valhalla or FMM if you want road segments.
- **T-Drive:** it's continuous per-taxi logs with no trip boundaries or occupancy flag. You'd have to segment trips yourself. The sampling is also too sparse for fine-grained similarity.
- **San Francisco:** the occupancy flag lets you split trips cleanly, but the sampling is coarse.

**Skip** NYC TLC, Chicago and Uber Movement. They only have pickup/drop-off or aggregated speeds, not point sequences. GeoLife has real trajectories but comes from 182 people, mostly walking and transit, not taxis.

Porto alone meets your "few hundred vehicles" bar, so I'd start there. Add T-Drive or Didi for cross-city generalization. I can write a loader and cleaning script for Porto if that would help.

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
I found no open or free-download dataset that lets you follow workers across firms with firm identifiers. Every usable option needs an application, and the realistic ones take weeks to months. Search results from the data registries were mostly noise, so the access facts below come from the agency pages (checked 2026-11-12) unless I say "from memory".

## What I assumed you need
- **R1:** a panel of at least 10 years.
- **R2:** a worker ID and a firm ID on every job spell.
- **R3:** enough job movers to give a large connected set.
- **R4:** wages or earnings for each job.
- I assumed any country is fine, that you can wait for an application, and that you have no affiliation with a particular country's institutions.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Size / span | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [MCVL (Spain)](https://portaldatos.seg-social.gob.es/mcvl) | Application, free, non-commercial research; weeks | Worker sample, annual waves (from memory: 4% sample, since 2004) | Strong on R1–R3; earnings are capped | Today (page); sample size from memory |
| 2 | [LIAB (Germany)](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/integrated-establishment-and-individual-data/liab/) | Application, on-site or remote desktop with vetted output; weeks to months | Daily biographies 1975–2024 | Strong, but selective sample | Today |
| 3 | [SIAB (Germany)](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/) | The downloadable file needs a use agreement; the version with establishment IDs is on-site or remote only | Biographies from 1975 | Partial | Today |
| 4 | [Veneto Worker Histories (Italy)](https://www.frdb.org/en/dati/dati-inps-carriere-lavorative-in-veneto/) | Signed form emailed to the foundation that distributes it; weeks | 1975–2001 | Good for methods, but ends in 2001 | Today |
| 5 | [Admin3 (Hungary)](https://adatbank.krtk.mta.hu/en/2020/02/) | Data request form; tied to KRTK researchers; months | 2003–2017 | Strong data, hard to access | Today, partly |
| 6 | [LEHD (US)](https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/) | Research data center proposal; 6–12+ months | Quarterly earnings, state-based | Strong, slow | Today |
| 7 | [Statistics Denmark IDA](https://dst.dk/en/TilSalg/Forskningsservice/Dataadgang/Autorisering) | Needs a Danish host institution; months | From memory: from 1980 | Strong, but needs a host | Access today, coverage from memory |

## Details
- **MCVL (Spain), my pick for a second-year student.** Institutions that justify non-commercial research can request it, and the Social Security data portal has an online form. A directorate there must approve it, and one academic source mentions about 11 forms (it may have changed). Employer episodes are identified by the employer's social-security account code. Contributions are capped, which understates the top of the distribution, and that matters for rising inequality. You must cite the directorate and send them your outputs. Research rooms in Madrid, Barcelona and Albacete are an alternative. The weeks-level timing is my estimate, not something I confirmed.
- **LIAB (Germany).** Workers come from firms in the IAB Establishment Panel. Firms with up to 49 employees contribute all workers, and larger firms contribute a 20% sample. You pick one base period per project (1993–2000, 2000–2007, 2007–2017 or 2014–2024). The biographies run 1975–2024. The page says the FDZ will provide AKM effects for 1985–2023 on request, which is a useful check on your own estimates. The page doesn't say whether researchers abroad can use it (the FDZ's international network, IDAN, may be the route), so email the FDZ before you plan around it.
- **SIAB (Germany).** The page says the downloadable file has no establishment identifiers, so you can't run AKM on it. The version that has them is on-site or remote only. The 2% sample size is from memory.
- **Veneto (Italy).** The foundation's page says to "fill and sign the attached form" and email it. It has worker and firm files with firm tax codes. A 2018 INPS paper says access is free. It stops in 2001, so it can't speak to recent inequality trends. It does give you full AKM data to build and test your code.
- **Admin3 (Hungary).** The page describes it as 2003–2017, with a successor database (Admin4) described in a 2026 working paper. The access pages suggest you need a KRTK researcher as co-author or supervisor, and the same pages cover several datasets, so confirm the Admin3 terms.
- **LEHD (US).** You work in a secure research data center after Census approval, and the proposal must show a benefit to Census. A regional center's page quotes 6–12 months or more.
- **Denmark IDA.** The statistics office only authorises Danish institutions, so foreign researchers need a Danish host.

## Known, not confirmed
I only searched the web for these and have no verified record.
- **Finland (FLEED).** Population-wide employer-employee data. Foreign access is possible, but remote access needs a Finnish affiliation and business data are often on-site only (old source).
- **Sweden (MONA).** Online remote platform. I found no current rules for foreign researchers.
- **Norway.** The remote system serves researchers with a Norwegian ID.
- **Canada (CEEDD).** Access through Statistics Canada's research data centers or its Centre for Data Development and Economic Research. Researchers cover the full cost (older source).
- **Portugal (Quadros de Pessoal).** Ask the labor ministry's planning office. I found no formal procedure. The Banco de Portugal route appears restricted to the bank's researchers (2018 guide).
- **France, Netherlands, Austria.** Not searched; from memory, restricted-access data exist for all three.

## Not recommended
- **Brazil public RAIS.** It is open, but de-identified, so you can't follow workers across years. The identified version needs a request to the Ministry of Labour and a cooperation agreement.
- **SIAB Campus File.** Free, but teaching only, with no publications allowed.
- **LEHD public aggregates (QWI, LODES, J2J).** No worker histories.
- **Replication packages for the Taiwan and Brazil AKM papers.** Useful as code, but the microdata are restricted. The pages blocked my automated checks.

## What I could not find
- An open worker-by-firm panel with identified firms.
- Current foreign-researcher rules for Sweden, Norway and Finland.

## Next step
**What you can start on today:**

Judge votes✓ ✓ ✓
Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
I found no open or free-download dataset that lets you follow workers across firms with firm identifiers. Every usable option needs an application, and the realistic ones take weeks to months. Search results from the data registries were mostly noise, so the access facts below come from the agency pages (checked 2026-11-12) unless I say "from memory".

## What I assumed you need
- **R1:** a panel of at least 10 years.
- **R2:** a worker ID and a firm ID on every job spell.
- **R3:** enough job movers to give a large connected set.
- **R4:** wages or earnings for each job.
- I assumed any country is fine, that you can wait for an application, and that you have no affiliation with a particular country's institutions.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Size / span | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [MCVL (Spain)](https://portaldatos.seg-social.gob.es/mcvl) | Application, free, non-commercial research; weeks | Worker sample, annual waves (from memory: 4% sample, since 2004) | Strong on R1–R3; earnings are capped | Today (page); sample size from memory |
| 2 | [LIAB (Germany)](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/integrated-establishment-and-individual-data/liab/) | Application, on-site or remote desktop with vetted output; weeks to months | Daily biographies 1975–2024 | Strong, but selective sample | Today |
| 3 | [SIAB (Germany)](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/) | The downloadable file needs a use agreement; the version with establishment IDs is on-site or remote only | Biographies from 1975 | Partial | Today |
| 4 | [Veneto Worker Histories (Italy)](https://www.frdb.org/en/dati/dati-inps-carriere-lavorative-in-veneto/) | Signed form emailed to the foundation that distributes it; weeks | 1975–2001 | Good for methods, but ends in 2001 | Today |
| 5 | [Admin3 (Hungary)](https://adatbank.krtk.mta.hu/en/2020/02/) | Data request form; tied to KRTK researchers; months | 2003–2017 | Strong data, hard to access | Today, partly |
| 6 | [LEHD (US)](https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/) | Research data center proposal; 6–12+ months | Quarterly earnings, state-based | Strong, slow | Today |
| 7 | [Statistics Denmark IDA](https://dst.dk/en/TilSalg/Forskningsservice/Dataadgang/Autorisering) | Needs a Danish host institution; months | From memory: from 1980 | Strong, but needs a host | Access today, coverage from memory |

## Details
- **MCVL (Spain), my pick for a second-year student.** Institutions that justify non-commercial research can request it, and the Social Security data portal has an online form. A directorate there must approve it, and one academic source mentions about 11 forms (it may have changed). Employer episodes are identified by the employer's social-security account code. Contributions are capped, which understates the top of the distribution, and that matters for rising inequality. You must cite the directorate and send them your outputs. Research rooms in Madrid, Barcelona and Albacete are an alternative. The weeks-level timing is my estimate, not something I confirmed.
- **LIAB (Germany).** Workers come from firms in the IAB Establishment Panel. Firms with up to 49 employees contribute all workers, and larger firms contribute a 20% sample. You pick one base period per project (1993–2000, 2000–2007, 2007–2017 or 2014–2024). The biographies run 1975–2024. The page says the FDZ will provide AKM effects for 1985–2023 on request, which is a useful check on your own estimates. The page doesn't say whether researchers abroad can use it (the FDZ's international network, IDAN, may be the route), so email the FDZ before you plan around it.
- **SIAB (Germany).** The page says the downloadable file has no establishment identifiers, so you can't run AKM on it. The version that has them is on-site or remote only. The 2% sample size is from memory.
- **Veneto (Italy).** The foundation's page says to "fill and sign the attached form" and email it. It has worker and firm files with firm tax codes. A 2018 INPS paper says access is free. It stops in 2001, so it can't speak to recent inequality trends. It does give you full AKM data to build and test your code.
- **Admin3 (Hungary).** The page describes it as 2003–2017, with a successor database (Admin4) described in a 2026 working paper. The access pages suggest you need a KRTK researcher as co-author or supervisor, and the same pages cover several datasets, so confirm the Admin3 terms.
- **LEHD (US).** You work in a secure research data center after Census approval, and the proposal must show a benefit to Census. A regional center's page quotes 6–12 months or more.
- **Denmark IDA.** The statistics office only authorises Danish institutions, so foreign researchers need a Danish host.

## Known, not confirmed
I only searched the web for these and have no verified record.
- **Finland (FLEED).** Population-wide employer-employee data. Foreign access is possible, but remote access needs a Finnish affiliation and business data are often on-site only (old source).
- **Sweden (MONA).** Online remote platform. I found no current rules for foreign researchers.
- **Norway.** The remote system serves researchers with a Norwegian ID.
- **Canada (CEEDD).** Access through Statistics Canada's research data centers or its Centre for Data Development and Economic Research. Researchers cover the full cost (older source).
- **Portugal (Quadros de Pessoal).** Ask the labor ministry's planning office. I found no formal procedure. The Banco de Portugal route appears restricted to the bank's researchers (2018 guide).
- **France, Netherlands, Austria.** Not searched; from memory, restricted-access data exist for all three.

## Not recommended
- **Brazil public RAIS.** It is open, but de-identified, so you can't follow workers across years. The identified version needs a request to the Ministry of Labour and a cooperation agreement.
- **SIAB Campus File.** Free, but teaching only, with no publications allowed.
- **LEHD public aggregates (QWI, LODES, J2J).** No worker histories.
- **Replication packages for the Taiwan and Brazil AKM papers.** Useful as code, but the microdata are restricted. The pages blocked my automated checks.

## What I could not find
- An open worker-by-firm panel with identified firms.
- Current foreign-researcher rules for Sweden, Norway and Finland.

## Next step
**What you can start on today:**
1. Write and test your AKM pipeline on simulated worker–firm data: connected-set pruning, high-dimensional fixed effects, and variance decomposition with a bias correction for limited mobility (e.g. Kline–Saggio–Sølvsten). These tools exist from memory; I did not check them here.
2. Read the replication code from the Taiwan and Brazil papers.

**Applications:**
- Start the MCVL application now.
- In parallel, email the German research data center about LIAB access from abroad.
- Ask your advisor whether anyone has a Danish, Hungarian or US research data center link.

The interactive comparison page is at `/private/tmp/e-G1qLVr/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

## Details
- **MCVL (Spain), my pick for a second-year student.** Institutions that justify non-commercial research can request it, and the Social Security data portal has an online form. A directorate there must approve it, and one academic source mentions about 11 forms (it may have changed). Employer episodes are identified by the employer's social-security account code. Contributions are capped, which understates the top of the distribution, and that matters for rising inequality. You must cite the directorate and send them your outputs. Research rooms in Madrid, Barcelona and Albacete are an alternative. The weeks-level timing is my estimate, not something I confirmed.
- **LIAB (Germany).** Workers come from firms in the IAB Establishment Panel. Firms with up to 49 employees contribute all workers, and larger firms contribute a 20% sample. You pick one base period per project (1993–2000, 2000–2007, 2007–2017 or 2014–2024). The biographies run 1975–2024. The page says the FDZ will provide AKM effects for 1985–2023 on request, which is a useful check on your own estimates.
